title: HTTP State Management Mechanism
summary: This document specified HTTP cookies: the Cookie and Set-Cookie headers that let a server keep state across requests. It differed from Netscape's earlier cookie proposal but could interoperate with it. It is historic and was replaced by RFC 2965.

plainLanguage.summary: A website hands you a numbered ticket on your first visit and asks to see it each time you come back.

questions: how do cookies work in http
subtitle: The standard mechanism for servers to store state on clients across multiple HTTP requests.

tldr.problem: HTTP requests are independent; a server cannot remember previous requests or recognize a returning user. Web applications need to maintain sessions for shopping carts, login state, and personalization.
tldr.mechanism: A server sends a Set-Cookie response header with a name-value pair and optional attributes (domain, path, expiration). The client stores it and returns it in a Cookie request header with each subsequent request. This RFC standardized cookies beyond Netscape's original implementation.
tldr.outcome: Cookies became the standard session mechanism in HTTP. This RFC is Historic and was replaced by RFC 2965.

today: RFC 2965 obsoletes this RFC. Cookies remain the dominant web session mechanism, though with additional standards like RFC 6265 (Cookie semantics and mechanics) providing updated guidance. The HTTP-only and SameSite attributes, and secure cookie practices, have evolved since this original specification.

sections.title: The Problem of Stateless HTTP
sections.content:
HTTP is stateless: each request is independent. A web server responds to a user's login request without knowing whether the user visited before or will visit again. For applications that need to maintain state across requests—a shopping cart, a login session, or personalization preferences—this is a problem.

This RFC specifies a standard way for servers to store small pieces of state on the client, called cookies. A server sends a Set-Cookie header with a name and value, the client stores it, and sends it back in subsequent requests via a Cookie header. This creates the illusion of a stateful session.
sections.plainLanguage: HTTP is like a store where nobody knows who you are each time you walk in. Cookies let the store give you a membership card you carry and show each visit.

sections.title: Set-Cookie and Cookie Headers
sections.content:
A Set-Cookie response header has the form Set-Cookie: NAME=VALUE; attributes. The NAME=VALUE pair is required. Optional attributes include:

  • Domain: restricts the cookie to a specific domain (e.g., .example.com)
  • Path: restricts the cookie to a path prefix (e.g., /shopping)
  • Max-Age: lifetime of the cookie in seconds; omitted means discard when the user agent exits
  • Secure: send the cookie only over HTTPS
  • Version: the specification version (1 for this RFC)

When the client sends a request, it includes a Cookie header with the applicable cookies, along with their Version, Path, and Domain attributes so the server can validate them.
sections.plainLanguage: The cookie is a slip of paper with a name and value. It can say 'remember me here' (domain), 'remember me on this section of the site' (path), and 'forget me in an hour' (expiration).

sections.title: Cookie Management and Behavior
sections.content:
A user agent stores cookies and applies rules for when to send them. A cookie is sent with a request only if the request's host matches the cookie's Domain attribute and the request's path matches the cookie's Path attribute. If a new Set-Cookie has the same NAME, Domain, and Path as an existing cookie, it replaces the old one. If Max-Age is zero, the cookie is discarded.

User agents have practical limits: at least 300 cookies total, at least 4096 bytes per cookie, and at least 20 cookies per host. Applications should use few and small cookies. For privacy, users should be able to see, disable, and delete cookies.
sections.plainLanguage: The client remembers the ticket, writes down when to throw it away, and hands it back only when visiting the right store and the right part of the store.

sections.title: Practical Deployment
sections.content:
Servers should divide content into application areas and use the Path attribute to distinguish them. Large state should be encoded as a key to a server-side database rather than stored entirely in the cookie. Servers should set appropriate cache headers (Cache-Control: no-cache="set-cookie", Expires: old-date) to prevent intermediaries from caching Set-Cookie headers, which would cause the same cookie to be sent to all clients.

Clients should use simple logout by sending Set-Cookie: NAME=VALUE; Max-Age=0 to delete a cookie. Shopping-cart and login-state cookies should usually be discarded when the user agent exits (no Max-Age set) to reduce privacy risks. The RFC distinguishes 'verifiable' transactions (user initiated) from 'unverifiable' ones (automatic redirects or embedded objects) and restricts cookie sending in unverifiable transactions to prevent cross-site leaks.
sections.plainLanguage: Servers should clean up their caches so everyone doesn't get everyone else's tickets. Clients should throw away important tickets when the user closes the browser.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Trade-Offs
sections.content:
Clear-text risk: Cookies travel in plain text in HTTP headers. Sensitive information (session IDs, authentication tokens) should be sent only over HTTPS to prevent interception.

Cookie spoofing: A malicious server in domain evil.com cannot forge a cookie for bank.com, because the Domain attribute restricts where cookies apply. However, servers in the same domain (e.g., a.evil.com and b.evil.com) can share cookies, so applications must validate that a cookie came from them and was not spoofed.

Privacy: Servers can track users across pages within their domain by setting different cookies or varying cookie content. The RFC requires user agents to give users control: the ability to disable cookies entirely, to view and delete them, and to be notified before a stateful session begins.
sections.plainLanguage: Tickets are readable to anyone snooping on the network; use HTTPS for important ones. One store cannot fake another store's ticket, but parts of the same store can trick each other. Users should be able to see and delete tickets.
